meta.description: Not Einstein. The exact wording traces to physicist John Archibald Wheeler’s 1979 tribute describing Einstein’s working method — then got mis-credited to Einstein.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'In the middle of difficulty lies opportunity'?
meta.ogDescription: No source shows Einstein saying it. The phrasing comes from physicist John Archibald Wheeler in 1979, describing Einstein — not quoting him.

answer.label: Not Albert Einstein — coined by physicist John Archibald Wheeler
answer.sourceLine: The precise wording first appears in a 1979 tribute by physicist John Archibald Wheeler, who listed it as one of the “rules of Einstein’s work” — his own paraphrase of Einstein’s approach, not a quotation from Einstein. Later writers dropped Wheeler’s name and credited the line directly to Einstein.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: In the middle of difficulty lies opportunity

source.excerpt: There are three additional rules of Einstein’s work that stand out for use in our science, our problems, our times … In the middle of difficulty lies opportunity.
trail: 1903 — the underlying idea circulates: a Christian Science newsletter carries A. P. Barton’s “Suggest to yourself an opportunity in every difficulty,” per Quote Investigator ↗.
1979 — the exact wording first appears in physicist John Archibald Wheeler’s Newsweek tribute “The Outsider,” as one of his “rules of Einstein’s work,” documented by Quote Investigator ↗.
1980 — a Hartford Courant column repeats the three rules but credits them straight to Einstein, dropping Wheeler; this is where the misattribution takes hold, per Quote Investigator ↗.
Today — the line is a fixture of Einstein quote collections such as Goodreads ↗, with no primary Einstein source ever cited.
source.cutTag: ↑ Wheeler’s words about Einstein — not a quotation from Einstein
source.excerptNote: In his 1979 Newsweek tribute, physicist John Archibald Wheeler distilled what he saw as Einstein’s working philosophy into three “rules.” The third rule is the line now universally hung on Einstein himself.
source.rightsNote: The exact 1979 wording is the work of John Archibald Wheeler and is not public domain. There is no verified Einstein original text to reproduce.

author.name: John Archibald Wheeler
author.heading: About John Archibald Wheeler
author.bio: John Archibald Wheeler was a leading American theoretical physicist known for work on general relativity, nuclear fission, and quantum information, and for popularizing the term “black hole.” A younger colleague and admirer of Einstein at Princeton, Wheeler distilled Einstein’s working style into three “rules” in a 1979 tribute — the source of the phrase now misremembered as Einstein’s own.

misattribution.heading: The attribution problem
misattribution.intro: This is one of the most reproduced “Einstein” lines online, but the trail leads to another physicist entirely.

items.why: No letter, essay, interview, or speech by Einstein — in German or English — has ever been produced containing this line. The wording first surfaces in 1979, decades after his death, as physicist John Archibald Wheeler’s paraphrase of Einstein’s method, per Quote Investigator ↗.

items.who: “In the middle of every difficulty lies opportunity”
items.why: A common inserted-word variant still credited to Einstein; it shares the same broken chain of custody and no primary source, as shown by Quote Investigator ↗.

misattribution.truthLine: The exact phrasing is best credited to John Archibald Wheeler (1979), who wrote it while describing Einstein — and the broader “difficulty is opportunity” sentiment predates them both, appearing as early as 1903, per Quote Investigator ↗.

context.heading: Why it stuck to Einstein
lead: The line rings true as “Einstein” because it was literally written about Einstein — Wheeler was characterizing the mind of the man he admired. Once a 1980 newspaper column reprinted the three rules and attached them directly to Einstein, the attribution snowballed through motivational books and, later, the internet.

The sentiment itself is older and more diffuse than either physicist. Versions of “every difficulty is an opportunity” circulated in the early twentieth century, which is why the idea feels timeless even though this exact sentence has a traceable 1979 origin.
context.pull: It was written about Einstein — which is exactly why it got mistaken for Einstein.
